title: Vision Zero in NYC
text:
Evaluating the Impact of Vision Zero Interventions on Pedestrian Casualties in NYC (2013-2023)
Motor vehicle crashes are a leading cause of death and injury in New York City (NYC). In 2014, the city adopted the Vision Zero (VZ) framework, a comprehensive strategy to eliminate all traffic-related fatalities. The program uses a multi-faceted approach, including infrastructure redesign, lower speed limits, and public awareness campaigns. This analysis evaluates the impact of nine distinct street-level interventions on pedestrian casualties. The study examines data from 2013 to 2023, focusing specifically on intersections that received treatments between 2015 and 2021. This approach ensures that every intervention can be evaluated with at least two years of ‘before’ data and two years of ‘after’ data, allowing for a robust comparison.








Key Findings

 Speed is Key  Interventions that physically slow traffic, like Neighborhood Slow Zones (-18%), were most effective.


 Unintended Harm  Signal Retiming to improve vehicle flow was linked to a 7% increase in casualties.


 Mixed Results  Other common treatments showed no significant citywide impact on pedestrian safety.







What Are the Vision Zero Interventions?
The analysis focuses on nine key physical and regulatory changes made to NYC streets. The table below provides a brief description of each intervention.








Descriptions of Assessed Vision Zero Interventions


Intervention
Description
Components / Examples




Citywide Speed Limit Reduction
Default speed limit change from 30 MPH to 25 MPH.
Streets may be signed or unsigned.


Enhanced Crossing
A marked high-visibility crosswalk on calm streets with low vehicle volumes, high pedestrian traffic, and no traffic signal or stop sign.
At minimum, include high visibility crosswalk markings, daylighting on all approaches, Americans with Disabilities Act compliant pedestrian ramps, and pedestrian warning signage.


Leading Pedestrian Interval Signal
Signals that show a pedestrian walk sign before showing a green light to vehicle traffic in the same direction, giving pedestrians a head start to cross the street before car traffic.
NA


Neighborhood Slow Zone
Neighborhood areas, selected based on crashes, presence of schools, and other factors, in which the speed limit has been reduced to 20 mph.
Include road markings and signs indicating entrance to a slow zone, along with greater concentration of other interventions.


SIP Corridors
Safety-oriented engineering improvements that use multiple treatments in a street corridor.
Examples: large range of subtypes, including markings, vertical elements, signage and regulatory changes, signal changes, concrete, and landscaping.


SIP Intersection
Safety-oriented engineering improvements that use multiple treatments in a single intersection.
Same as above, but within intersections rather than along street corridors.


Speed Hump
A raised area of a roadway designed to reduce vehicle speeds.
NA


Turn Traffic Calming
A traffic calming measure that guides drivers to turn more safely and increases pedestrian visibility.
Examples: hardened centerline, slow turn wedge, bike island channelization, median extension.


25 MPH Signal Retiming
A corridor where the signal progression has been changed to match the 25 MPH speed limit.
NA









Map of All Vision Zero Interventions



The interactive map on the right displays the polygon geometry for every intersection in NYC. Zoom-in and click on any intersection to see a list of the Vision Zero interventions it has received and the year each was first implemented.
Note: This map displays ALL intersections in the city, including ones which were left out of our statistical modeling.













Citywide Pedestrian Casualty Trends
To understand the citywide context, we first examined the overall trend in pedestrian casualties across all 9,562 intersections in our study.



The number of pedestrian casualties showed a general downward trend over the study period, with a sharp, anomalous drop in 2020. This dip corresponds to the major changes in traffic patterns and pedestrian activity during the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic.
While casualties rebounded after 2020, they remained below pre-pandemic levels, suggesting that Vision Zero initiatives may be contributing to a sustained, long-term improvement in pedestrian safety.











The following charts break this down further. Each plot shows the casualty trend for intersections that ever received a particular type of intervention. This helps visualize trends within specific treatment groups and reveals that the overall citywide pattern is largely consistent across different intervention types.








Vision Zero Implementation Timeline
The Vision Zero program was rolled out in a staggered fashion, with different intersections receiving treatments in different years. Our study design leverages this staggered implementation to better isolate the causal impact of each intervention.



Nearly 25% of intersections in our data received their first Vision Zero intervention in 2016, with 2,247 intersections treated during that year.
No intersection in our data received its first Vision Zero treatment in 2021, suggesting that the program’s implementation to new intersections might have been limited in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic.













Intervention-Specific Rollout
To see how each specific safety measure was rolled out over time, the charts below break down the implementation timeline for each of the nine interventions studied. Each chart shows the number of intersections that received that particular treatment for the first time in a given year. Notice how some interventions, like Neighborhood Slow Zones, were implemented heavily towards the beginning of the program’s roll-out, while others, like Street Improvement Corridors, were deployed throughout the observation period.
While the program’s expansion to new intersections paused in 2021, the work itself did not. The charts below reveal a strategic shift: instead of expanding the program’s footprint, the city began deepening the investment by layering additional safety measures onto intersections that were already part of the program.








Impact of VZ Interventions on Pedestrian Safety
Instead of just looking at intersections before and after a treatment, our staggered difference-in-difference design does something smarter: it compares the change in casualties at a treated intersection to the change in casualties at similar intersections that hadn’t received that treatment yet.
We used a negative binomial regression model to estimate the effect of each intervention on the annual count of pedestrian casualties. The results are presented as an Incidence Rate Ratio (IRR). An IRR below 1.0 suggests the intervention reduced casualties, while an IRR above 1.0 suggests it increased them.
The table below summarizes these findings. Rows are colored based on the result: green for a statistically significant reduction, red for a significant increase, and grey for no significant effect.

Ranking Intervention Effectiveness


The bar chart visualizes the estimated percent change in pedestrian casualties for each intervention, providing an at-a-glance summary of which strategies were most effective.

What Works Best? The most successful interventions manage vehicle speed through physical design or regulation.

Neighborhood Slow Zones (-18.4%)
Turn Traffic Calming (-14.4%)
Speed Humps (-11.5%)

What Doesn’t Work (or Makes Things Worse)?

25 MPH Signal Retiming (+7.1%) was the only intervention associated with a harmful effect.
Leading Pedestrian Intervals, Enhanced Crossings, and SIP Intersections had no statistically significant effect.















Conclusion & Policy Implications
Our analysis confirms that Vision Zero has had a tangible, positive impact on pedestrian safety, but not all interventions contribute equally. The findings provide a clear mandate for future transportation policy:

Prioritize Speed Management: The most effective way to protect pedestrians is to control vehicle speed. Future investments should be heavily focused on expanding infrastructure like Neighborhood Slow Zones, Turn Traffic Calming, and Speed Humps.
Re-evaluate Signal Retiming: The finding that signal retiming to favor vehicle flow is associated with an increase in pedestrian casualties is alarming. Transportation agencies must carefully review this practice and consider pairing it with other proven safety measures.
Focus on Systemic, Not Spot, Treatments: Redesigning an entire street segment (SIP Corridors) was effective, while implementing similar projects at a single intersection was not. This suggests that creating a consistently safe environment along an entire corridor is more impactful than isolated, spot-based fixes.

Ultimately, this research shows that building a safe transportation system and an efficient one are not conflicting goals. Investments in traffic calming are a core component of an efficient network that is safer and more predictable for all.


About the Data & Analysis
This analysis was conducted by the NYC Council Data Team using publicly available data from NYC Open Data, including datasets from the NYPD and the Department of Transportation. The full methodology is detailed in our to-be-published manuscript.
While our statistical model controls for many factors, traffic safety is incredibly complex. The findings represent our best estimate of the impact of these specific interventions, but other unmeasured factors could also play a role.

Must meet all three: How to name files - Jennifer Bryan

Machine-readable
Human-readable
Sortable





dataset-name_time-granularity_grouping_year.extension



Lower case underscore naming convention
Descriptive file names
An underscore separates the different descriptors
Hyphens are used in place of spaces within descriptors

Descriptors

Order file should be run (00-10)
Dataset Name, Source, Location
Time granularity (hourly, daily, minutely, yearly, etc.)
Grouping categorizer ex ‘by-age’, ‘by-cd’, ‘by-cd-age’
Date or Year

Examples:

acs_unemployment_by-cd_2018.csv
:cry: N_per_day_age_pop.csv → :partying_face: nys_doc-population_daily_by-age








No dots in variables names (not python friendly)
Lower case underscore naming convention
Descriptive
Comment first use of variable (if not completely obvious)








Functions and prior scripts should be referenced at the top of every file.
Each file should do one thing.

Functions or complicated cleaning or scraping should be put into its own script.

Often is a .R or .PY script

There can be a file that calls or references previous files. (One file to run it all or to produce final outputs)

Often is a .RMD or .IPYNB or bash file


Avoid hard-coding values into your code.
Recommend DRY code. Turn repeated code into a function that takes the changes as parameters.
Files that depend on other files require a numbered file name.








Delineate sections of code
Explain parameter choices of functions or hard-coded values
Explain first use of variable (if not completely obvious)







There are two types of repositories: project and collection.
For project repositories:

Each data request is its own repo.
The Readme, About, and Tags are filled out.
No passwords are ever shown on a repo.
If there is no private data, then repo is destined to be public.
When cleaning up a repo, old, unused code/data/visuals can be placed into an ‘archived’ called folder.

Vision Zero in New York City
Motor vehicle crashes are a leading cause of death and injury in New York City (NYC). In 2014, the city adopted the Vision Zero (VZ) framework, a comprehensive strategy to eliminate all traffic-related fatalities. The program uses a multi-faceted approach, including infrastructure redesign, lower speed limits, and public awareness campaigns.

Key Findings at a Glance



Our analysis reveals a clear pattern: interventions that physically or legally force drivers to slow down are the most effective at protecting pedestrians.

 Effective Interventions: Five interventions led to statistically significant reductions in pedestrian casualties, with Neighborhood Slow Zones (-18%) and Turn Traffic Calming (-14%) showing the largest safety benefits.


 Adverse Interventions: One intervention, 25 MPH Signal Retiming, was associated with a significant 7% increase in pedestrian casualties, highlighting a potential unintended consequence of prioritizing vehicle flow.


 No Significant Effect: Three interventions, including Leading Pedestrian Interval signals and single-intersection improvement projects (SIPs), showed no detectable citywide impact on pedestrian casualties.
